data.abstract: In this paper, to bridge the gap between physical knowledge and learning approaches, we propose an induced current learning method (ICLM) by incorporating merits in traditional iterative algorithms into the architecture of convolutional neural network (CNN). The main contributions of the proposed method are threefold. First, to the best of our knowledge, it is the first time that the contrast source is learned to solve full-wave inverse scattering problems (ISPs). Second, inspired by the basis-expansion strategy in the traditional iterative approach for solving ISPs, a combined loss function with multiple labels is defined in a cascaded end-to-end CNN (CEE-CNN) architecture to decrease the nonlinearity of objective function, where no additional computational cost is introduced in generating extra labels. Third, to accelerate the convergence speed and decrease the difficulties of the learning process, the proposed CEE-CNN is designed to focus on learning the minor part of the induced current by introducing several skip connections and to bypass the major part of induced current to the output layers. The proposed method is compared with the state-of-the-art of deep learning scheme and a well-known iterative ISP solver, where numerical and experimental tests are conducted to verify the proposed ICLM.

data.title: Physics-Inspired Convolutional Neural Network for Solving Full-Wave Inverse Scattering Problems
data.venue: IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation

data.abstract: Electromagnetic inverse scattering problems (ISPs) under limited-aperture conditions pose significant challenges due to data incompleteness and increased nonlinearity. This paper proposes Limited Aperture Network (LA-NET), a novel network for electromagnetic ISPs with limited-aperture data (90°-360°). Without retraining, LA-NET predicts permittivity, scattered field, and induced current using wavelet-compressed inputs and a physics-informed unrolling mechanism. By reducing input dimensionality and incorporating physical priors, it lowers computational cost and improves reconstruction quality. Numerical and experimental results show that LA-NET outperforms existing methods in adaptability and robustness across varying apertures.

data.title: Physics-Inspired Quantitative Computational Imaging Utilizing Sensors with Constrained Apertures

data.abstract: This paper proposes a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) framework for solving inverse scattering problems, enabling rapid and accurate reconstructions under diverse measurement conditions. In the proposed approach, the dielectric property is represented as a learnable tensor, while a neural operator is employed to predict the induced current distribution. A hybrid loss function, consisting of the state loss, data loss and total-variation (TV) regularization, is constructed to establish a fully differentiable formulation for a joint optimization of network parameters and dielectric property. To demonstrate the framework's generality and flexibility, PINO is implemented using three representative neural operators, i.e., the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO), the enhanced Fourier Neural Operator (U-FNO) and the Factorized Fourier Neural Operator (F-FNO). Compared with conventional approaches, the proposed framework offers a simpler formulation and universal modeling capability, making it readily applicable to various measurement scenarios, including multi-frequency and phaseless inversion. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed PINO achieves high accuracy and robust reconstruction across samples with and without phase information, under single-frequency and multi-frequency settings in the presence of noise. The results demonstrate that PINO consistently outperforms conventional contrast-source inversion (CSI) methods and provides an efficient, unified solution to complex electromagnetic inverse-scattering problems.

data.title: Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Electromagnetic Inverse Scattering Problems

data.abstract: Physics-driven neural solvers can reconstruct strongly nonlinear inverse scattering scenes without supervised training, but their per-instance optimization over pixelwise unknowns is computationally expensive. This letter presents a fast physics-driven Fourier-spectral solver for 2-D transverse-magnetic inverse scattering. The induced current is parameterized in a truncated Fourier basis, so that the reconstruction is carried out in a compact spectral space rather than on dense spatial grids. To improve robustness in high-contrast regimes, a contraction integral equation is incorporated into the physics-consistency model. In addition, a contrast-compensated operator is introduced to alleviate boundary attenuation caused by spectral truncation, and a bridge-suppressing loss is designed to reduce false connections between adjacent scatterers. A lightweight fully connected network, initialized from a back-propagation-based estimate, optimizes the spectral coefficients for each measurement instance. Numerical examples and Fresnel experimental data show that the proposed method preserves the main target topology and quantitative contrast with subsecond reconstruction time. Compared with representative spatial-domain physics-driven solvers, it achieves nearly two orders of magnitude acceleration while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality, which is promising for fast microwave imaging applications.

data.title: A Fast Physics-Driven Fourier-Spectral Solver for Highly Nonlinear Inverse Scattering Problems
data.venue: IEEE Antennas and Wireless Propagation Letters

data.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have recently been applied to inverse scattering problems (ISPs) due to their strong nonlinear mapping capabilities. However, supervised DNN solvers require large-scale datasets, which limits their generalization in practical applications. Untrained neural networks (UNNs) address this issue by updating weights from measured electric fields and prior physical knowledge, but existing UNN solvers suffer from long inference time. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a contrast-source-based physics-driven neural network (CSPDNN), which predicts the induced current distribution to improve efficiency and incorporates an adaptive total variation loss for robust reconstruction under varying contrast and noise conditions. The improved imaging performance is validated through comprehensive numerical simulations and experimental data.
